source_text:
De fide
̓Επιφανίου Κύπρου ἐκ τοῦ περὶ πίστεως λόγου.
Καὶ ἵνα δείξῃ, ὅτι "μεσίτης" ἐστὶ "θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων" τὰ ἀμφότερα ἔχων, ἐξ
ἀνθρώπων μὲν τὴν σάρκα, ἐκ δὲ πατρὸς τὴν ἀόρατον οὐσίαν, λαλεῖ μὲν ὡς θεὸς τὰ
θεῖα καὶ θεοπρεπῆ, ὡς δὲ ἄνθρωπος ὁ αὐτὸς τὰ ἀνθρώπινα καὶ ἀνθρωποπρεπῆ, ἔχων
ἐν ἀμφοτέροις τὴν ἐξουσίαν φυσικῶς καὶ οὐσιωδῶς, ἀσυγχύτως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως,
θεϊκῶς τε καὶ ἀνθρωπίνως.
pass_a_gloss: Lemmatic heading naming Epiphanius of Cyprus and his treatise about belief. Then a purpose clause: in order to prove that Christ stands as go-between linking God with humanity, combining each nature in his own person. His body comes from the human race on one side; his unseen being comes from his Father on the other side. Speaking in his divine role, he utters sublime themes suited to reverence; speaking in his human role, that identical speaker utters everyday mortal themes. He exercises ruling power across each sphere by birthright and by substance, with no blending and no severance, operating at one moment in a heavenly fashion and at another in an earthly fashion.
pass_b_english: Of Epiphanius of Cyprus, from the discourse On Faith.

And to show that he is "mediator of God and men" (1 Timothy 2:5), holding both in himself — from men his flesh, and from the Father his invisible essence — as God he speaks what is divine and befitting God, and as man the same one speaks what is human and befitting man, holding authority in both naturally and essentially, without confusion and without division, in a divine manner and in a human manner.

choices.issue: Unstated subject of the purpose clause
choices.choice: Kept implicit (to show); the commentary context points to Pauline phrasing.
Inline parenthetical beside the mediator clause; quotation marks kept from the Greek.
The Father: the flesh/essence contrast requires the divine Father.

notes: Khazarzar; Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify
